title: Java & Spring — Illustrated Engineering Atlas
domain: Java fundamentals and Spring Framework / major Spring portfolio projects
scope: Depth 2: fundamentals and best practices for a working software engineer. 32 topics cover Java contracts and runtime, Framework core, Boot, web/data/security, messaging/integration/batch, Cloud, testing/observability and optional Modulith/AI/native/specialist capabilities. This is a broad mechanism atlas, not exhaustive documentation of every Spring API or cloud subproject. Java examples use non-preview constructs from modern Java (records require 16+; virtual threads 21+). Research anchors Java SE 25 and live Spring documentation retrieved 2026-10-09. The retrieved Boot system-requirements page reports Boot 4.1.1, Framework 7.0.9+, Java 17–26. Use the matching BOM and supported project generations; do not combine displayed individual project versions arbitrarily. Code snippets are illustrative and were not compiled as a complete application. Choices and improvements marked synthesis are reasoned recommendations, not measured performance results.

adaptations: Original Java/Spring content and editable semantic SVGs; no source-example branding.
Off-white paper, blue headings, yellow highlights, purple underline, exact five-family pastel palette.
Five curriculum bands in cover cards; four learning stages remain separately labeled.
Wide mechanism diagrams for readable code and relationships; notebook pages remain responsive.

topics.title: Java, Framework, Boot: find the layers
topics.takeaway: Know the owner of a behavior before debugging its annotations.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Learn which layer owns which concern. Java supplies the language and runtime. Framework supplies the container and application infrastructure. Boot assembles and configures applications. Portfolio projects add specialized capabilities.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: For a quote API, start with Java, Boot, MVC, Data and Security. Add Batch for overnight reconciliation; add messaging when asynchronous delivery is required. A portfolio is a toolbox, not a dependency shopping list.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Choose a compatible Boot generation first; let its dependency management align libraries. This reduces manual coordination but means an upgrade can change several components together.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: “All Spring” is too broad for exhaustive API coverage. This atlas teaches major mechanisms and maps specialist projects; it does not document every method or cloud provider integration.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Compare your actual dependency tree with the compatible project generations. Remove unused starters and track a reproducible runtime/build baseline.

figures.title: Which layer owns the behavior?
figures.alt: Java / JVM: language + runtime; Spring Framework: container + infrastructure; Spring Boot: assembly + configuration; Portfolio projects: Data / Security / Cloud. Connections: Spring Boot to Spring Framework (builds on); Spring Framework to Java / JVM (runs on); Portfolio projects to Spring Boot (integrates)
figures.caption: Layer arrows mean builds on or integrates with; they are not the path of an HTTP request.

check.question: Does Boot replace Framework?
check.answer: No. Boot builds on Framework and automates application setup.

topics.title: Types, objects, records and domain invariants
topics.takeaway: A type should make the wrong state harder to represent.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Separate primitive values from object references. An interface states a contract; a class implements behavior. Records express data aggregates with final component fields; they do not make referenced collections deeply immutable.

sections.heading: Worked example · illustrative, not executed
Engineering decision
sections.body: Use composition for replaceable pricing behavior and small value types for identifiers. This clarifies invariants at the cost of more explicit conversions.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: A final reference can point to a mutable object. Value equality also needs a compatible hashCode; identity equality with == answers a different question.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Move invalid-state checks into construction boundaries. Test equality, null handling and defensive copies where the business invariant depends on them.

figures.title: Why can a final reference still change?
figures.alt: Reference A: points to a list; Reference B: points to same list; Mutable list: shared object. Connections: Reference A to Mutable list (alias); Reference B to Mutable list (alias)
figures.caption: Reference identity and object state are different; defensive copies break unwanted sharing.

check.question: Is a record containing ArrayList deeply immutable?
check.answer: No. Its field reference is final, but the referenced list can remain mutable.

topics.title: Collections, generics and equality
topics.takeaway: Collection contracts are part of your domain contract.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Select the collection by its contract: List preserves a sequence, Set models uniqueness, Map associates keys and values. Hash-based containers rely on equality and hashing; HashMap does not promise iteration order.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A broker list preserves display order; a Set tracks unique coverage codes; a Map indexes quotes by stable QuoteId. Use a sorted map when sorted traversal is part of the requirement.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Prefer interface-typed variables and explicit generic parameters. Choose ArrayList for ordinary indexed sequences; choose a deque for queue/stack operations instead of treating one structure as universal.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Changing fields used by a key’s equality/hash after insertion can make lookup fail. Concurrent access needs a suitable concurrency strategy, not merely a different collection name.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Write down ordering, duplicate and mutation requirements before selection. Measure realistic access patterns before swapping structures for supposed performance gains.

figures.title: Which collection matches the invariant?
figures.alt: Requirement: What must stay true?; List: sequence + duplicates; Set: unique membership; Map: key → value. Connections: Requirement to List (ordered sequence); Requirement to Set (uniqueness); Requirement to Map (lookup by key)
figures.caption: These are contracts, not performance rankings. Implementation and workload determine cost.

check.question: Why are mutable map keys dangerous?
check.answer: Their hash/equality behavior may change after storage, so later lookup searches the wrong location.

topics.title: Lambdas, streams and honest parallelism
topics.takeaway: Readable transformation beats decorative functional syntax.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: A lambda implements a functional interface. A Stream describes a computation over a source: intermediate transformations are lazy, and a terminal operation consumes the pipeline. A stream is not a reusable collection.

sections.heading: Worked example · illustrative, not executed
Engineering decision
sections.body: Use streams for clear transformations and loops for stateful control flow or early branching. Parallel execution adds coordination overhead and is useful only with appropriate work and isolation.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Side effects inside map/filter make ordering and parallel behavior difficult to reason about. A parallel stream is not a safe way to issue unbounded database calls.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Start sequential. Benchmark representative inputs and examine thread usage before adopting parallelism; isolate blocking I/O with an explicit bounded execution policy.

figures.title: When does a stream actually execute?
figures.alt: Source: quotes; filter → map: lazy transformations; toList(): terminal traversal; Result list: materialized values. Connections: Source to filter → map (elements); filter → map to toList() (evaluated on demand); toList() to Result list (collect)
figures.caption: This is a sequential pipeline. Parallel execution requires separate assumptions about side effects and workload.

check.question: Why does filter alone produce no result?
check.answer: It is intermediate and lazy; a terminal operation such as toList triggers traversal.

topics.title: Resource ownership and decimal money
topics.takeaway: Memory, resources and money each need their own ownership rules.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Garbage collection does not replace deterministic resource closure. AutoCloseable integrates with try-with-resources. BigDecimal models decimal arithmetic, with explicit precision/rounding decisions and scale-sensitive equals.

sections.heading: Worked example · illustrative, not executed
Engineering decision
sections.body: Use decimal values or an explicitly specified minor-unit model for premiums. State currency, scale and rounding at business boundaries; neither approach chooses the policy for you.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: BigDecimal constructed from a binary double can inherit representation artifacts. Leaking file/database resources can exhaust capacity even when heap usage appears healthy.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Define resource ownership and close scope. Exercise rounding edges and failure paths; compare 1.0 and 1.00 with the intended numeric or representation semantics.

figures.title: What must be explicit at a boundary?
figures.alt: Owner scope: opens resource; Use resource: success or exception; close(): scope exits; Money policy: currency + rounding. Connections: Owner scope to Use resource (try-with-resources); Use resource to close() (always on exit)
figures.caption: Top: deterministic resource lifetime. Bottom: decimal policy is a separate domain decision.

check.question: Does BigDecimal.equals ignore scale?
check.answer: No. compareTo can test numeric equality; equals also distinguishes scale.

topics.title: Concurrency, visibility and virtual threads
topics.takeaway: Cheap waiting is not unlimited throughput.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Concurrency coordinates overlapping tasks. Visibility and atomicity are different: volatile can publish writes, but does not make read-modify-write increments atomic. Virtual threads make blocking I/O concurrency cheaper; they do not create CPU or database capacity.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: Two workers read count=0 and both write 1: one increment is lost. AtomicInteger or a lock can protect this invariant. For quote calls, a semaphore can bound access to a scarce insurer connection.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Use virtual threads for many blocking I/O tasks when dependencies fit. Bound downstream concurrency; use workload-appropriate executors for CPU work and decide timeout/cancellation ownership.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: A shared mutable singleton remains shared under virtual threads. Avoid pooling virtual threads. Pinning guidance is JDK-dependent; older synchronized pinning advice should not be repeated universally for newer JDKs.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Load-test with slow dependencies. Record pool wait, in-flight calls, CPU and tail latency; stop increasing concurrency when the constrained resource saturates.

figures.title: Where should concurrency be limited?
figures.alt: Many tasks: virtual threads; Semaphore: bounded admission; DB / insurer: scarce capacity; Waiting tasks: do not consume slots. Connections: Many tasks to Semaphore (request slot); Semaphore to DB / insurer (admitted work); Semaphore to Waiting tasks (no slot available)
figures.caption: Limit the scarce downstream resource. The figure illustrates admission control, not virtual-thread scheduling internals.

check.question: Does volatile count++ become atomic?
check.answer: No. Reading, adding and writing remain a compound operation.

topics.title: JVM, JIT, garbage collection and diagnosis
topics.takeaway: Observe the bottleneck before tuning the JVM.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: HotSpot starts with interpretation and adaptively compiles hot code. Garbage collection manages object memory. Flight Recorder captures runtime events for diagnosis; request latency can include CPU, allocation, locks and external waiting.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A quote endpoint’s latency rises while CPU stays modest. A recording and dependency timings may reveal contention or connection waits rather than expensive Java computation.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Choose a runtime and collector against workload and deployment limits. Compare warm steady-state behavior and startup separately; a microbenchmark rarely predicts full service latency.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Treating every pause as a GC problem can hide a slow database. Increasing heap can reduce some collection pressure while increasing footprint and changing pause behavior.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Form a hypothesis, capture JFR plus service metrics, change one factor, then repeat representative load. Keep the measurement environment and warm-up conditions explicit.

figures.title: How do execution and evidence connect?
figures.alt: Bytecode: loaded methods; Interpreter: execute + profile; JIT compilation: hot methods; Heap / GC: allocation + reclamation; JFR recording: runtime evidence. Connections: Bytecode to Interpreter (execute); Interpreter to JIT compilation (hot code); Interpreter to JFR recording (events); Heap / GC to JFR recording (events)
figures.caption: Simplified HotSpot view. JFR includes additional event categories; GC and compilation may run concurrently.

check.question: Can low CPU coexist with high latency?
check.answer: Yes. A request may be waiting for a lock, I/O or a scarce connection.

topics.title: IoC, constructor injection and bean definitions
topics.takeaway: The container should assemble your design, not become your design.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Inversion of control means the container constructs and connects collaborators. Dependency injection exposes what an object needs. Component scanning and @Bean methods are two ways to register bean definitions.

sections.heading: Worked example · illustrative, not executed
Engineering decision
sections.body: Use constructor injection for required collaborators. Use @Bean for third-party objects or explicit assembly; use qualifiers when multiple candidates represent meaningful alternatives.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Field injection hides required dependencies and complicates plain construction. Circular dependencies often signal tangled responsibilities; adding lazy references can conceal the design problem.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Construct business services directly in unit tests. Inspect candidate ambiguity and configuration boundaries before widening component scans.

figures.title: Who creates and connects collaborators?
figures.alt: ApplicationContext: bean definitions; Pricing adapter: implements PricingPort; QuoteService: requires PricingPort. Connections: ApplicationContext to Pricing adapter (construct); ApplicationContext to QuoteService (construct); Pricing adapter to QuoteService (inject reference)
figures.caption: Arrows distinguish construction from injecting an existing collaborator. Business calls are omitted.

check.question: Why inject an interface?
check.answer: It names a replaceable contract; the container supplies the selected implementation.

topics.title: Scopes, lifecycle and thread-safe singleton design
topics.takeaway: Scope controls lifetime; it does not grant thread safety.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: A singleton is one instance per bean definition per container. Request scope follows a web request. The container manages initialization/destruction for managed beans, with important exceptions such as prototype destruction.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: QuoteService may safely be a singleton when it stores only stable collaborators. A mutable currentTenant field would mix simultaneous requests; carry tenant context through an explicit request-level mechanism instead.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Keep shared service state immutable or deliberately synchronized. Choose scope by ownership and lifetime; request-scoped dependencies in singletons need appropriate proxies or lookup.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: @PostConstruct runs during initialization, before normal proxy-mediated use. Depending on transactional advice there is unsafe. Prototype cleanup is not automatically managed like singleton destruction.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Move external startup work into a suitable lifecycle stage. Test concurrent requests and shutdown; name who owns cleanup for prototype or manually created objects.

figures.title: When is a bean ready for advised calls?
figures.alt: Create bean: inject dependencies; Initialize target: lifecycle callbacks; Expose bean: possibly proxied; Destroy managed bean: shutdown callbacks. Connections: Create bean to Initialize target (populate); Initialize target to Expose bean (post-process); Expose bean to Destroy managed bean (container closes)
figures.caption: Typical simplified lifecycle. Prototype destruction and manually created objects require separate ownership.

check.question: Does singleton mean one instance across a cluster?
check.answer: No. Each application container has its own singleton instances.

topics.title: AOP proxies: why annotations sometimes vanish
topics.takeaway: An annotation is metadata; the invocation path makes it operational.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Spring AOP commonly intercepts calls through a proxy before reaching the target. JDK interface proxies and subclass proxies have different constraints. A target calling itself does not re-enter its Spring AOP proxy.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A controller invokes quoteService.issue(): transaction advice runs. Inside the target, this.audit() bypasses proxy interception, even if audit has an advice-triggering annotation.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Place independently advised operations on separate collaborators or use an explicit programmatic boundary. This adds a visible interface but avoids magical assumptions about annotation placement.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Subclass proxies cannot advise final/private methods as overridable methods. Calling a manually constructed object also bypasses container advice. AspectJ weaving is a different mechanism.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Test behavior through the managed bean and deliberately exercise self-invocation. Inspect actual proxy type and advice ordering when multiple concerns wrap one method.

figures.title: Which call crosses the proxy boundary?
figures.alt: Caller: managed reference; Proxy: transaction / other advice; Target issue(): business operation; Target audit(): self-invocation. Connections: Caller to Proxy (external call); Proxy to Target issue() (intercepted); Target issue() to Target audit() (this.audit() bypasses proxy)
figures.caption: Default Spring AOP proxy mode. A self-call does not return to the proxy; weaving can behave differently.

figures.title: How can an advised audit boundary become explicit?
figures.alt: QuoteService: issues policy; AuditService proxy: independent advice; Audit target: audit operation. Connections: QuoteService to AuditService proxy (injected collaborator); AuditService proxy to Audit target (proxy interception)
figures.caption: Proposed refactoring: call another managed collaborator. Select transaction propagation intentionally; separate beans alone do not select it.

check.question: Will this.audit() start a proxy-driven new transaction?
check.answer: Not in default proxy mode. The call stays within the target.

topics.title: Spring Boot: conditional assembly, not sorcery
topics.takeaway: Auto-configuration is conditional code you can inspect.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Boot auto-configuration uses available classes, properties and existing beans to configure infrastructure. User definitions can cause defaults to back off. Starters assemble related dependencies; dependency management aligns versions.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: Add a database driver and the relevant starter, supply connection properties, and Boot can create infrastructure beans. Define your own DataSource and the matching default may no longer apply.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Keep Boot-managed versions aligned unless an override has a documented reason. Select a supported runtime and build tool for your chosen generation.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: A starter can activate unexpected configuration. Mixing individual Spring versions may produce linkage errors. A bean declared too broadly can accidentally replace a useful default.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Use the condition evaluation report to understand why configuration matched or failed. Record custom overrides and test upgrades against startup and representative paths.

figures.title: Why was an infrastructure bean created?
figures.alt: Classpath: libraries present?; Properties: feature enabled?; Existing beans: user replacement?; Conditions evaluated: create or back off. Connections: Classpath to Conditions evaluated (class conditions); Properties to Conditions evaluated (property conditions); Existing beans to Conditions evaluated (bean conditions)
figures.caption: Conditions vary by auto-configuration. This figure shows the main inputs, not every condition type.

check.question: Does adding a starter guarantee a working database?
check.answer: No. Driver, credentials, reachable infrastructure and matching configuration still matter.

topics.title: Configuration, profiles and secret boundaries
topics.takeaway: Debug the effective configuration, not just the file you edited.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Boot combines ordered property sources into an Environment and binds structured configuration. Later/higher-precedence sources can override earlier values. Profiles select configurations; they are not a security boundary.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: For pricing.timeout, define a default and an environment-specific override. Bind settings into a typed ConfigurationProperties object and validate required values instead of scattering string lookups.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Treat operational settings as external inputs and make startup fail clearly on invalid required configuration. This improves repeatability but demands disciplined deployment configuration.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: An unexpected environment variable can override a checked-in value. Logging a full configuration dump can reveal secrets; a prod profile does not protect management endpoints.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Document the effective source and precedence for critical settings. Review secrets access separately and test startup with missing, malformed and overridden values.

figures.title: Which configuration value actually wins?
figures.alt: application.yml: baseline; Environment: deployment overrides; CLI / other sources: ordered inputs; Effective value: bind + validate. Connections: application.yml to Effective value (property sources); Environment to Effective value (property sources); CLI / other sources to Effective value (property sources)
figures.caption: The complete precedence order is documented in Boot. This diagram illustrates merging, not the whole ranked list.

check.question: Why might changing application.yml have no effect?
check.answer: A higher-precedence source can supply the same property.

topics.title: MVC request flow, DTO validation and errors
topics.takeaway: Validate syntax at transport boundaries and invariants in the domain.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: DispatcherServlet delegates request mapping and invocation to MVC components. Validation checks request constraints. Error handling can produce ProblemDetail responses rather than leaking internal exception representations.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: POST /quotes accepts a validated request DTO. The service enforces business eligibility; the repository persists. A validation failure returns a stable client error, while an internal failure gets a traceable sanitized response.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Keep controllers focused on transport and services on use-case policy. DTOs decouple API shapes from persistence; the additional mapping is an intentional boundary cost.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Bean Validation cannot prove business eligibility or authorization. Returning persistence entities can expose fields and trigger unexpected serialization-time loads.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Exercise malformed input, missing access and failure responses with HTTP tests. Keep stable problem types and correlate internal diagnostics without returning stack traces.

figures.title: Where do request responsibilities belong?
figures.alt: DispatcherServlet: route request; Controller + DTO: validate / translate; Service: business rules; Repository: persistence; Exception handling: ProblemDetail. Connections: DispatcherServlet to Controller + DTO (invoke handler); Controller + DTO to Service (use case); Service to Repository (data access); Controller + DTO to Exception handling (invalid input); Service to Exception handling (failure)
figures.caption: Request-side responsibilities; responses return through MVC. Authentication filters normally run before this view.

check.question: Can @Valid prove an agent owns a policy?
check.answer: No. Ownership is an authorization/domain rule, not just a field constraint.

topics.title: MVC, WebFlux and virtual threads: choose by constraints
topics.takeaway: Choose an execution model for your dependencies, not your fashion sense.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: MVC supports an imperative request model; WebFlux uses non-blocking composition and reactive backpressure. Mono represents zero-or-one values and Flux a sequence. Virtual threads provide a separate way to scale blocking waits.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A JPA quote API fits MVC naturally. A streaming aggregator with non-blocking downstream clients may fit WebFlux. Wrapping a blocking JPA call in Mono does not make its I/O non-blocking.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Choose based on dependency APIs, concurrency pattern and team expertise. MVC with virtual threads can retain readable blocking code; WebFlux adds composition and scheduling discipline.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Blocking an event loop can stall unrelated requests. A reactive return type alone does not identify the server stack, and virtual threads do not remove database limits.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Prototype the same realistic workload with bounded dependencies. Compare memory, tail latency and failure handling; adopt complexity only for a measured benefit.

figures.title: Which I/O contract fits the execution model?
figures.alt: MVC: request execution; Blocking driver: JDBC / JPA; Virtual threads: cheap blocking waits; WebFlux: event-loop processing; Non-blocking driver: async I/O + demand. Connections: MVC to Blocking driver (imperative I/O); Virtual threads to Blocking driver (still bounded); WebFlux to Non-blocking driver (reactive pipeline)
figures.caption: Two valid styles; virtual-thread configuration is separate from choosing MVC. No universal performance ranking is implied.

check.question: Does Mono.just(blockingCall()) defer that call?
check.answer: No. The argument is evaluated immediately before Mono.just receives it.

topics.title: Spring Data: repositories, aggregates and fetch plans
topics.takeaway: Repository convenience does not cancel database physics.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Spring Data builds repository abstractions around store-specific behavior. JPA has persistence-context and relationship semantics; Data JDBC uses a simpler aggregate model. Derived queries reduce boilerplate without replacing query design.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A broker dashboard pages quotes by tenant and status. Use a response projection and a deliberate fetch plan instead of traversing every policy relationship during JSON serialization.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Choose JPA when its entity model helps; choose JDBC-style access when explicit aggregate operations fit. R2DBC is a non-blocking access model, not reactive JPA.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: A compact repository method can still produce expensive SQL. N+1 access and loading oversized graphs should be diagnosed through executed queries and row counts, not annotation counts.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Capture SQL and query plans for representative tenant sizes. Validate pagination and fetch plans together; compare query count and end-to-end latency after changes.

figures.title: Where does repository abstraction stop?
figures.alt: Repository contract: query + aggregate intent; JPA model: context + relationships; JDBC model: explicit aggregates; Actual database: SQL + indexes + rows. Connections: Repository contract to JPA model (implementation); Repository contract to JDBC model (implementation); JPA model to Actual database (queries); JDBC model to Actual database (queries)
figures.caption: JPA and JDBC are alternatives shown together for comparison. They do not share a persistence context.

check.question: Is R2DBC just JPA returning Mono?
check.answer: No. It is a different non-blocking relational access model.

topics.title: Transactions, rollback and propagation boundaries
topics.takeaway: A local transaction is a precise boundary, not a universal undo button.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: @Transactional defines an advised transaction boundary. Default rollback typically covers unchecked exceptions and Error; checked-exception behavior can be customized, including global defaults. Read-only is generally a hint, not a universal write prohibition.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: An issuePolicy service method updates the quote and inserts the policy in one database transaction. An email call is not rolled back just because the database transaction fails.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Keep boundaries around coherent database use cases and avoid long remote waits while holding connections. Choose explicit rollback policy and account for propagation and pool capacity.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Self-invocation can bypass advice. Catching and swallowing a failure can prevent expected rollback. REQUIRES_NEW can require an additional connection and therefore worsen pool pressure.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Verify rollback through the proxied bean with real persistence. Exercise checked exceptions, concurrent conflicts and external side-effect failure separately.

figures.title: What does the transaction actually protect?
figures.alt: Transaction proxy: begin / participate; Database updates: quote + policy; Commit or rollback: configured rules; External email: outside DB atomicity. Connections: Transaction proxy to Database updates (invoke service); Database updates to Commit or rollback (method outcome); Database updates to External email (side effect risk)
figures.caption: One database transaction. Reactive transaction context, distributed coordination and propagation need separate treatment.

check.question: Will a database rollback unsend an email?
check.answer: No. External effects need separate coordination such as durable events and idempotent handling.

topics.title: Security filters, JWT and domain authorization
topics.takeaway: Authentication names the caller; authorization constrains the action.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: SecurityFilterChain applies authentication and authorization to matching servlet requests. A resource server verifies bearer tokens and derives authorities; accepting a decoded token is not equivalent to verifying it.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: With Keycloak as issuer, validate the JWT signature, issuer and applicable claims. Convert claims deliberately, then check that the authenticated agent may access the requested tenant’s policy.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Keep identity-provider responsibilities separate from application resource rules. Token authorities can express permissions, but row/tenant ownership still belongs in enforceable application logic.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: A valid token can target another tenant’s resource. Incorrect matcher order can leave a route under the wrong filter chain. Configure audience requirements rather than assuming they are always enforced automatically.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Test anonymous, expired, wrong-issuer, wrong-audience and cross-tenant requests. Inspect granted authorities and deny access consistently at the relevant resource boundary.

figures.title: Where does identity become resource access?
figures.alt: HTTP request: bearer token; SecurityFilterChain: verify + authenticate; Authorities: mapped claims; Resource decision: permission + tenant. Connections: HTTP request to SecurityFilterChain (matched chain); SecurityFilterChain to Authorities (authenticated identity); Authorities to Resource decision (authorize use case)
figures.caption: Servlet resource-server example. Token verification and per-resource authorization are separate decisions.

check.question: Does a valid JWT authorize every policy ID?
check.answer: No. The application must enforce permission and ownership for that resource.

topics.title: Sessions, browser credentials and CSRF
topics.takeaway: Understand how credentials travel before disabling protections.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Spring Session externalizes session handling through shared implementations. CSRF is about a browser automatically attaching credentials to a forged request; it is not solved by calling the API “REST.”

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A browser broker portal uses a session cookie and CSRF token on state-changing requests. Two app replicas can access shared session state instead of relying solely on one process’s memory.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Choose session or bearer-token flows from client and threat requirements. Shared sessions improve replica mobility but introduce storage availability, expiration and serialization concerns.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Stateless does not automatically mean CSRF-safe if browser credentials are still sent automatically. CORS policy is not a replacement for CSRF protection.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Exercise expiration, logout, replica changes and state-changing cross-origin requests. Confirm credential behavior and token checks for the actual browser flow.

figures.title: How do sessions survive replica changes?
figures.alt: Browser: cookie + CSRF token; App replica A: session integration; App replica B: session integration; Shared session store: expiry + state. Connections: Browser to App replica A (request); Browser to App replica B (next request); App replica A to Shared session store (load / save); App replica B to Shared session store (load / save)
figures.caption: A shared session store is an option, not mandatory for every app. CSRF still depends on credential transport.

check.question: Why can a cookie API need CSRF protection?
check.answer: Because a browser can automatically attach the cookie to a forged request.

topics.title: Caching: keys, freshness and invalidation
topics.takeaway: Every cache needs an owner, a key contract and a freshness promise.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Spring’s cache abstraction delegates storage to a backing implementation. @Cacheable can reuse results; eviction and updates define freshness behavior. An annotation alone does not define TTL or make a distributed cache consistent.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: For a policy summary, use a key containing tenant and policy ID. Evict or update affected summaries after successful policy changes under an explicitly chosen consistency policy.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Cache expensive, repeatedly read data with an acceptable staleness budget. Choose local versus shared storage by consistency, footprint and latency requirements.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Missing tenant identity in a key can reuse another tenant’s data. Default proxy-based caching also has self-invocation limits. Cache invalidation and database commit ordering need care.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Measure hit ratio, stale reads and miss cost. Exercise concurrent misses and updates; bound entry size and TTL using the provider’s configuration.

figures.title: What happens on a cache hit and miss?
figures.alt: Read request: tenant + policy ID; Cache lookup: complete key; Return cached value: hit; Database load: miss; Populate cache: provider policy. Connections: Read request to Cache lookup (lookup); Cache lookup to Return cached value (hit); Cache lookup to Database load (miss); Database load to Populate cache (loaded result)
figures.caption: Cache-aside conceptual flow. TTL, stampede control and update consistency are provider/application choices.

check.question: Does @Cacheable itself choose a TTL?
check.answer: No. Expiration is generally a backing-cache/provider concern.

topics.title: Kafka, AMQP and Pulsar: delivery boundaries
topics.takeaway: Assume retries can repeat business work unless your boundary proves otherwise.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Spring messaging integrations connect templates and listeners to broker-specific behavior. Kafka transactions can cover a read/process/write Kafka sequence; this does not universally make external database or HTTP side effects exactly once.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A PolicyIssued event may be redelivered. A consumer records a stable event ID and performs its database change atomically where feasible, avoiding a second business effect on retry.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Use messaging to decouple timing and absorb work under explicit delivery rules. Choose the broker by ordering, routing, retention and operational requirements rather than a universal winner.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Acknowledging before durable processing can lose work; acknowledging afterward can allow redelivery. “Exactly once” must name the protected boundary, and poison-message retries need a finite outcome.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Test a crash after the effect but before acknowledgement. Track lag, retries and dead-letter handling; verify deduplication with the actual transaction and broker configuration.

figures.title: Where can a duplicate become a second effect?
figures.alt: Broker event: event ID = E42; Consumer: process + deduplicate; Business store: effect + event marker; Acknowledge / commit: after chosen boundary. Connections: Broker event to Consumer (delivery / redelivery); Consumer to Business store (durable effect); Consumer to Acknowledge / commit (processing outcome)
figures.caption: Application-level idempotency sketch; broker protocols and acknowledgement semantics differ.

check.question: Does Kafka EOS make an HTTP payment exactly once?
check.answer: No. The external payment needs its own idempotency and coordination contract.

topics.title: Spring Integration: adapters, channels and routing
topics.takeaway: A diagrammed integration flow still needs a capacity model.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Spring Integration models messages passing through channels and endpoints. Adapters connect external systems; transformers change representation; routers select destinations. Channel type affects threading and delivery behavior.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: An inbound insurer file adapter emits messages. A transformer normalizes records; a router sends valid records to underwriting and malformed ones to a review destination.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Use integration flows when multiple protocols and routing rules need explicit composition. Prefer a direct service call for a simple local interaction; each extra channel adds behavior to understand.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Assuming every channel is asynchronous misreads the execution model. A slow endpoint can block a synchronous flow; unbounded asynchronous handoff can merely move overload into memory.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Choose and document channel capacity and error handling. Simulate slow consumers and malformed messages; inspect queue depth, rejection behavior and recovery ownership.

figures.title: How does one input become two processing paths?
figures.alt: Inbound adapter: file / external source; Transformer: normalize message; Router: evaluate record; Underwriting channel: accepted records; Review channel: malformed records. Connections: Inbound adapter to Transformer (message channel); Transformer to Router (normalized message); Router to Underwriting channel (valid); Router to Review channel (invalid)
figures.caption: Enterprise integration pattern example; channels can be synchronous or asynchronous.

check.question: Is every Spring Integration channel async?
check.answer: No. Channel implementation determines handoff and threading behavior.

topics.title: Spring Batch: chunk commits and safe restarts
topics.takeaway: Restartability is a data contract, not a checkbox.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: A Job contains Steps; chunk-oriented processing reads items, optionally processes them, and writes a chunk at a commit interval. Job/Step execution metadata distinguishes logical instances, attempts and restart state.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: An overnight reconciliation job handles rows in chunks. If a later chunk fails, previously committed chunks remain; restart behavior depends on metadata and the components’ restart contracts.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Choose chunk size against transaction duration, memory and write cost. Use stable job parameters and restartable input ordering; external side effects still need deliberate idempotency.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: A restarted job is not equivalent to replaying every row from zero. Changing input between attempts or losing execution metadata can break assumptions and duplicate effects.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Fail a run deliberately halfway through. Verify which chunks commit and which rows resume; measure processing rate, skip/retry counts and resource contention.

figures.title: What survives a batch failure?
figures.alt: ItemReader: read records; ItemProcessor: transform / filter; ItemWriter: write chunk; Chunk commit: durable boundary; JobRepository: execution metadata. Connections: ItemReader to ItemProcessor (items); ItemProcessor to ItemWriter (chunk items); ItemWriter to Chunk commit (commit interval); Chunk commit to JobRepository (record progress)
figures.caption: Conceptual chunk and metadata responsibilities; transaction participation depends on actual repository/resource configuration.

figures.title: Which work remains after a failed chunk?
figures.alt: Chunks 1–7: committed work; Chunk 8: failed / rolled back; Restart: resume per contract; Execution metadata: saved progress. Connections: Chunks 1–7 to Chunk 8 (later processing); Chunk 8 to Restart (new execution); Execution metadata to Restart (restart state)
figures.caption: Conceptual restart boundary. Stable input, restartable components and durable metadata are required; external effects need idempotency.

check.question: Does failure in chunk 8 undo chunks 1–7?
check.answer: Normally no. Each completed chunk already committed within its own transaction boundary.

topics.title: Spring Cloud: select distributed capabilities
topics.takeaway: Distribute deliberately; pay the network bill consciously.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Cloud projects supply distributed patterns: Config, Gateway, discovery, LoadBalancer, Circuit Breaker, Stream, Function and Task. Release trains coordinate compatible dependencies with a BOM.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A gateway routes broker requests; a service calls an insurer using an HTTP client. On Kubernetes, evaluate whether platform discovery/configuration already supplies the needed capability before adding another layer.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Use RestClient for blocking calls, WebClient for reactive composition, or HTTP Service Clients for declarative interfaces. OpenFeign remains feature-complete; maintainers recommend HTTP Service Clients for new evolution.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Cloud abstractions do not remove network failures or distributed consistency problems. The old docs/current Cloud URL can expose an old train; match documentation to the actual version.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Map each component to one operational need. Verify Boot/Cloud compatibility and timeout behavior, then remove duplicate discovery, routing or configuration responsibilities.

figures.title: Which distributed responsibility needs a component?
figures.alt: Client: broker portal; Gateway: routing policies; Application service: domain use case; Insurer service: HTTP contract; Configuration source: operational settings. Connections: Client to Gateway (request); Gateway to Application service (route); Application service to Insurer service (bounded client call); Configuration source to Application service (configuration)
figures.caption: Illustrative deployment, not a mandatory Cloud stack. Compatibility is governed by the selected release train.

check.question: Should every Kubernetes service add Eureka?
check.answer: No. First determine whether native discovery already meets the requirement.

topics.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC and hypermedia
topics.takeaway: Transport changes the contract shape; business rules still need enforcement.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: API styles expose different contracts. REST centers resources and HTTP semantics; GraphQL executes a schema-selected field graph; gRPC defines RPC services/messages. Spring HATEOAS helps express links and affordances in representations.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A broker dashboard asks GraphQL for policies and owners. Request-scoped DataLoader batching can collect owner IDs, reducing repeated lookups without turning the API into one unrestricted database query.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Choose REST for familiar interoperable resource APIs, GraphQL for client-shaped graphs, and gRPC for typed RPC requirements. Consider client support, evolution, authorization and observability alongside payload size.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: GraphQL can hide N+1 fetching and expensive query shapes. Changing transport does not supply per-field/resource permissions. Hypermedia links should reflect permitted actions rather than grant authority themselves.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Measure query cost and downstream calls. Enforce workload limits and compatible contract evolution; keep authentication, authorization and deadline behavior explicit for each transport.

figures.title: How does GraphQL avoid repeated owner loads?
figures.alt: GraphQL selection: policies + owners; Field resolvers: owner keys; DataLoader: batch within request; Backing service: bounded lookup. Connections: GraphQL selection to Field resolvers (execute fields); Field resolvers to DataLoader (collect loads); DataLoader to Backing service (batch lookup)
figures.caption: One GraphQL mechanism. REST and gRPC are contract alternatives, not stages of this flow.

check.question: Does DataLoader guarantee one query for the entire request?
check.answer: No. It batches compatible loads; actual queries depend on keys, resolvers and backing implementation.

topics.title: Tests that catch wiring, persistence and HTTP failures
topics.takeaway: Test the boundary where the defect can actually occur.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Boot supports focused test slices and full-context tests. A slice loads a constrained subset; a full application test exercises broader wiring. Different scopes answer different questions.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: Test pricing rules with ordinary objects; validate controller errors with an MVC slice; exercise repository mappings against a representative database; reserve full application tests for critical integration flows.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Pick the cheapest test that can detect the targeted failure. Real infrastructure tests cost time but can expose SQL, serialization and configuration problems that mocks cannot.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: A mocked repository cannot establish real transaction rollback. Test-managed transactions can also conceal commit-time behavior; choose the test boundary to match the production failure.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Build a few high-value scenarios: authorization denial, conflict/rollback, malformed requests and startup misconfiguration. Track failure relevance rather than chasing coverage percentage alone.

figures.title: Which test can prove the behavior?
figures.alt: Unit test: rule correctness; Slice test: selected framework boundary; Integration test: real infrastructure; Critical HTTP flow: application behavior. Connections: Unit test to Critical HTTP flow (rule confidence); Slice test to Critical HTTP flow (binding confidence); Integration test to Critical HTTP flow (persistence confidence)
figures.caption: These are complementary test scopes, not a required execution chain. Full-context does not automatically mean real external services.

check.question: Can an MVC slice validate real database rollback?
check.answer: Not by itself. It typically excludes the persistence infrastructure required to prove it.

topics.title: Actuator, observations, metrics and traces
topics.takeaway: A dashboard earns its place by answering a failure question.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Actuator exposes operational endpoints under explicit exposure/security settings. Micrometer Observation can support metrics and tracing. Low-cardinality dimensions suit metric aggregation; high-cardinality identifiers can explode metric series.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: Observe quote latency by route template and outcome. Correlate a slow request through a trace; inspect database wait and JVM events instead of placing every policy ID in a metric label.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Design signals around an operational question: errors, latency, saturation and dependency behavior. Expose only required management capabilities and restrict sensitive endpoints.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Health is not one universal status. Putting shared external outages into liveness can trigger needless restarts; readiness dependencies should reflect whether this instance can serve useful traffic.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Simulate slow insurer calls and database outages. Confirm traces propagate and alerts identify the constrained boundary; measure signal cardinality and retention costs.

figures.title: Which signal answers which question?
figures.alt: HTTP operation: named observation; Metrics: bounded dimensions; Trace spans: request causality; Actuator endpoints: health + operational access; Runtime recording: CPU / locks / allocation. Connections: HTTP operation to Metrics (aggregate); HTTP operation to Trace spans (correlate)
figures.caption: Metrics aggregate, traces connect work, runtime recordings explain JVM behavior. Endpoint exposure is a separate security decision.

check.question: Should policyId be a metric label?
check.answer: Usually no. Its high cardinality can create excessive time series; use logs/traces appropriately.

topics.title: Timeouts, retries, bulkheads and scheduled work
topics.takeaway: Resilience protects a budget; it does not promise eventual success.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Framework 7 has core retry and concurrency-limit facilities with explicit enabling. Circuit breakers address repeated dependency failure. Executors run tasks; schedulers decide when to trigger them. @Async commonly relies on proxy invocation.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: An insurer times out after receiving a quote request. Retry only under an idempotency contract; otherwise a successful but lost response can lead to duplicate work.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Set an overall deadline, per-attempt budgets and bounded concurrency. Retry selected transient failures with backoff/jitter; a fallback must preserve honest business semantics.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Retries amplify overload. The new Framework retry API and older Spring Retry have different packages/settings. Scheduled work can run on every replica unless coordination is explicitly designed.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Inject latency, partial failure and response loss. Measure total attempts and deadline breaches; verify limits protect dependencies and that failed work has an observable final outcome.

figures.title: When does retry improve reliability?
figures.alt: Overall deadline: finite budget; Concurrency limit: protect dependency; Dependency call: per-attempt timeout; Retry decision: transient + safe?; Final outcome: success or explicit failure. Connections: Overall deadline to Concurrency limit (admit); Concurrency limit to Dependency call (attempt); Dependency call to Retry decision (failure); Retry decision to Concurrency limit (bounded retry); Dependency call to Final outcome (success / exhausted)
figures.caption: Policy sketch, not annotation execution order. Retry and transaction nesting must be chosen deliberately.

check.question: Is retrying every failure always safer?
check.answer: No. Permanent failures waste capacity, and non-idempotent operations may repeat side effects.

topics.title: Modulith: enforce domain boundaries before distribution
topics.takeaway: Make boundaries real before making them remote.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Spring Modulith derives application modules from a Boot application structure and supports boundary verification. Modules expose APIs/named interfaces while keeping implementation details internal.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: Separate quotes, policies and billing into modules. Quotes calls the published policy API or emits a domain event; it should not reach directly into billing’s internal persistence package.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Use a modular monolith when one deployment can satisfy operational needs. This preserves local interactions while clarifying boundaries, but independent scaling/deployment may later justify extraction.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Package names alone cannot prevent coupling if public internals are widely imported. Replacing calls with events changes consistency and failure semantics; it is not automatically an improvement.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Run module dependency verification and focused module tests. Track coupling and change ownership before extracting a service; choose extraction based on an actual deployment constraint.

figures.title: What is a legitimate module dependency?
figures.alt: Quotes module: internal rules; Policies API: published boundary; Policies internals: private implementation; Billing module: separate responsibility. Connections: Quotes module to Policies API (allowed dependency); Policies API to Policies internals (implementation); Policies API to Billing module (explicit collaboration)
figures.caption: Logical domain boundaries inside one process. The figure does not imply separate services or databases.

check.question: Does Modulith require microservices?
check.answer: No. It is designed to structure modules within a Spring Boot application.

topics.title: Spring AI: retrieval and tools with controlled authority
topics.takeaway: The model can suggest an action; the application must authorize it.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Spring AI offers model, embedding, vector-store and tool abstractions. RAG retrieves context for generation; tools let the model request application capabilities. The application executes those capabilities and owns the resulting authority.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: An assistant retrieves permitted policy wording and drafts an explanation. A requested issuePolicy tool must still validate the agent, tenant, eligibility and required approval in ordinary application code.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Use the framework to integrate models, not to outsource business authorization. Retrieval improves grounding under suitable data and chunking, but cannot guarantee factual correctness.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Retrieved text and model output can be untrusted. A tool exposed to a model may have real side effects; prompt wording alone cannot enforce access rules or prevent repeated operations.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Build a small evaluation set covering wrong-tenant retrieval, unsupported answers and unsafe tool requests. Trace sources and measure correctness, latency and cost before broadening capabilities.

figures.title: Who owns authority when the model calls a tool?
figures.alt: User question: authenticated caller; Authorized retrieval: tenant-scoped context; Model: answer / tool request; Application tool gate: validate + authorize; Business service: controlled action. Connections: User question to Authorized retrieval (retrieve); Authorized retrieval to Model (augment prompt); Model to Application tool gate (requested tool); Application tool gate to Business service (only if allowed)
figures.caption: Proposed guarded design grounded in Spring AI mechanisms; application authorization is not supplied by retrieval itself.

check.question: Does retrieved context make every answer true?
check.answer: No. Retrieval can be incomplete or wrong, and generation can still misinterpret it.

topics.title: AOT and native images: optimize the deployment case
topics.takeaway: Optimize the lifecycle that dominates your real cost.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: Native images compile under a closed-world assumption. Spring AOT analyzes application assembly ahead of runtime and generates supporting assets. Dynamic bean-graph changes and reflection/resource access can require different handling.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: A rarely invoked quote utility may benefit from reduced startup overhead. A long-running service may favor JVM JIT behavior; measure both against the actual deployment workload.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Evaluate native deployment when startup and footprint constrain the product. Accept build complexity and compatibility work only when the measured operational benefit matters.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: A successful JVM run does not prove native compatibility. Runtime configuration that changes which beans exist can conflict with build-time assembly assumptions.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Test the native artifact itself, including serialization, resources and integrations. Compare cold start, steady-state throughput, memory and build time under equivalent conditions.

figures.title: What moves from runtime into the build?
figures.alt: Application + config: build inputs; Spring AOT: analyze + generate assets; Native build: closed-world analysis; Native executable: runtime behavior; Artifact tests: real integrations. Connections: Application + config to Spring AOT (analyze); Spring AOT to Native build (generated support); Native build to Native executable (execute); Native executable to Artifact tests (verify)
figures.caption: Simplified native-image pipeline; ahead-of-time processing and compilation are distinct steps.

check.question: Can native mode freely rebuild its bean graph from runtime properties?
check.answer: No. AOT/closed-world constraints limit runtime changes to application assembly.

topics.title: Specialist Spring projects: choose the protocol
topics.takeaway: Use the smallest set of projects that honors your actual contracts.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: The portfolio includes specialist tools: Web Services for contract-first SOAP, LDAP for directory access, HATEOAS for links, REST Docs for tested documentation, Shell for CLIs and Web Flow for controlled navigation.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: Use SOAP integration for an insurer’s fixed XML contract; LDAP when identity data lives in a directory. Use REST Docs to connect documented API examples to tests rather than maintaining unrelated examples manually.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Match the external contract first, then select the adapter/framework. Specialized projects reduce plumbing but add protocol and lifecycle knowledge; they are not mandatory for every Boot application.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: An older tutorial may reference an Attic project as if it were a current default. Attic status requires checking migration/replacement guidance; it is not a blanket statement about every existing deployment.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Inventory specialty protocols and historical dependencies. Read each selected project’s current support and migration notes before adoption or replacement.

figures.title: Which specialist fits the requirement?
figures.alt: External requirement: protocol or workflow; SOAP contract: Spring Web Services; Directory access: Spring LDAP; Resource links: Spring HATEOAS. Connections: External requirement to SOAP contract (XML schema); External requirement to Directory access (directory contract); External requirement to Resource links (hypermedia contract)
figures.caption: These are alternatives for distinct needs. REST Docs, Shell and Web Flow add other focused capabilities.

check.question: Should a REST-only service add Spring Web Services?
check.answer: Usually no. Its purpose is SOAP/XML-oriented service integration.

topics.title: A production learning loop and migration compass
topics.takeaway: Learn the mechanism, state the constraint, measure the change.

sections.heading: Goal & mental model
sections.body: A compatible runtime and framework baseline makes behavior reproducible. Verification spans business rules, framework wiring and operating signals. Portfolio status and compatibility documentation should guide version-sensitive choices.

sections.heading: Worked example · design exercise
sections.body: Baseline a quote service, add one change such as a fetch plan or concurrency limit, and repeat representative load and failure scenarios. Keep the result only when it improves the target without breaking invariants.

sections.heading: Engineering decision
sections.body: Start with one well-observed modular service. Add distributed components, caching, reactive execution or native compilation when a specific constraint justifies the complexity.

sections.heading: Pitfall & diagnosis
sections.body: Installing every project is not ecosystem mastery. A change that lowers average latency while worsening failure recovery or tenant isolation may be a regression.

sections.heading: Improve & validate
sections.body: Study in order: Java contracts → container/proxies → HTTP/data/security → failure handling → optional capabilities. Record expected benefit, measurement and rollback criteria for every production change.

figures.title: How does a better service become a proven service?
figures.alt: Baseline: known behavior; Hypothesis: one named constraint; One change: mechanism + cost; Measure + fail-test: correctness + operability; Decision: keep / revise / revert. Connections: Baseline to Hypothesis (observe); Hypothesis to One change (propose); One change to Measure + fail-test (validate); Measure + fail-test to Decision (assess); Decision to Baseline (new baseline)
figures.caption: This is an engineering synthesis, not a claim of measured performance gains for the example service.

check.question: When should a new abstraction be adopted?
check.answer: When its mechanism addresses a named constraint and evidence shows its benefit outweighs its cost.
